content: Multicellular organisms are composed of more than one cell, with these cells being specialized to perform distinct functions. Most visible life forms, as well as all members of the Plantae and Animalia kingdoms, are multicellular, with the exception of certain specialized organisms like Myxozoans in the Animalia kingdom. The organization of multicellular organisms occurs at several hierarchical levels: Differentiated Cells The simplest living multicellular organisms, such as sponges, are composed of various specialized cell types that work together to achieve a common purpose. These cell types include: Choanocytes: Cells responsible for digestion. Sclerocytes: Cells that secrete structural support materials. Porocytes: Tubular cells that form pores. Pinacocytes: Epidermal cells that form the outer layer. Although these cells collectively form the macroscopic structure of a sponge, they do not create true interconnected tissues. This is evident from the fact that if a sponge is mechanically disaggregated (e.g., blended), its surviving cells can reassemble into a functional sponge. However, individual cell types cannot survive independently. In contrast, simpler colonial organisms like Volvox consist of cells that are free-living and capable of surviving independently if separated from the colony. Tissues More complex organisms, such as jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones, exhibit a tissue level of organization. In these organisms, differentiated cells are interconnected and work together as a group to perform specialized functions. For example: Jellyfish have an epidermis and a nerve net that provide protective and sensory functions. They also have an inner gastrodermis, which is responsible for digestion. The spatial arrangement of these differentiated cells is a key focus of anatomical studies. Organs and Organ Systems In even more complex organisms, tissues combine to form organs, which are structures designed to perform specific functions. Examples of organs include: The brain of a flatworm, which is a simple cluster of ganglion cells. The stem of a sequoia tree, which can grow up to 90 meters (300 feet) tall. The vertebrate liver, which is highly complex and multifunctional. The most advanced multicellular organisms, such as mammals, trees, and flowering plants, possess organ systems. These systems consist of groups of organs that work together to perform intricate, interrelated functions. For instance, in the vertebrate digestive system: The mouth and esophagus are responsible for ingesting food. The stomach crushes and liquefies the food. The pancreas and gallbladder produce and release digestive enzymes. The intestines absorb nutrients into the bloodstream. Evolutionary History The oldest known multicellular organism that has been taxonomically identified is a red alga called Bangiomorpha pubescens. Fossils of this organism have been found in rocks dating back 1.2 billion years to the Ectasian period of the Mesoproterozoic era. For multicellular organisms to reproduce, they must regenerate an entire organism from germ cells (sperm and egg cells). This process is a central focus of developmental biology. The emergence of sexual reproduction in unicellular organisms during the Ectasian period is believed to have been a critical factor in the evolution and proliferation of multicellular life. Multicellular organisms also face unique challenges, such as cancer. Cancer arises when cells lose the ability to regulate their growth and deviate from the normal developmental program.
